title: Weather Watch
objectives: I can use weather words to describe the weather outside.
I can tell the difference between a breeze and a storm.
I can use foggy, chilly, and damp to say exactly how it feels.
I can tell why the weather made something happen.
rationale: Weather is the first topic where first graders describe the world exactly, so the unit mixes a science word (weather) with everyday words (storm, breeze) and richer describing words (foggy, chilly, damp). Each describing word replaces a vague one (bad, cold, wet), which gives children a reason to choose a better word. The unit revisits describe, because, and happen, since children describe the weather and explain what it made happen.

passage.title: A Foggy Morning
paras: The weather was strange this morning. A storm came last night, so the grass is damp. Now the air is foggy and chilly, and Ana cannot see the tall tree. She feels a small breeze on her face. She zips up her coat because it is cold. Soon the sun will come out.

qs.why: The story says a storm came last night.

qs.q: Why does Ana zip up her coat?
qs.why: The air is chilly, and the story says she zips her coat because it is cold.

qs.q: In the story, what does foggy mean?
choices: Hard to see through because of mist
qs.why: Ana cannot see the tall tree, so foggy means mist makes it hard to see.

teacher.overview: Children learn six words to describe the weather and use them in a short description. The unit revisits describe, because, and happen from earlier units.

notes.va.weather.n: Weather is what the air is like outside, today. Start the day with a weather chart and let children choose a word. It is not the same as climate; keep it to today.
notes.va.storm.n: Make a storm in the classroom with sounds: tap fingers for rain, stomp for thunder. Contrast with breeze on the same wind line.
notes.va.breeze.n: Use a paper strip and gentle blowing to show a breeze. Children often say wind for everything; give breeze as a better word for a soft wind.
notes.va.foggy.adj: Make a foggy picture with a white crayon cover. Ask 'What can you not see?' Link fog and foggy: the y adds 'having fog'.
notes.va.chilly.adj: Put chilly on a thermometer line between warm and cold. Children often confuse chilly with freezing; chilly is only a little cold.
notes.va.damp.adj: Use a dry sponge and a damp sponge. Damp is a little wet, not soaking. Link to the opposite word dry.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'I look outside. The weather is gray. I feel a breeze, but it is not a storm. The grass is damp because it rained. The air is chilly, so I wear a jacket. It is foggy, so I cannot see the hill. I can describe the weather using these words.'
discuss: How is a breeze different from a storm?
What happens to the grass after a storm?
misconceptions: A breeze is the same as a storm.
extend: Children keep a three-day weather journal using one new word each day.
Children act as weather reporters and describe the weather in front of a picture.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit foggy, chilly, and damp the next day with a new picture, again at one week, and use weather words in morning meeting. They return in the animal habitats unit.

wida.oral: Partner A looks at a weather picture and describes it with two words from the unit. Partner B guesses which picture and says what to wear.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (el tiempo, tormenta, brisa, con niebla, fresco, húmedo) are not reviewed by a native speaker; foggy and chilly have several possible Spanish words.
The wind ladder (calm, breeze, wind, storm) is an informal scale for first graders, not a scientific one.
